title: Biggest Lottery Winners by State: Powerball's Luckiest
description: From a 24-year-old in Wisconsin to an 84-year-old in Florida, meet the real people behind Powerball's biggest jackpots — and what happened next.
content:
The Morning Everything Changed

Mavis Wanczyk didn't wait until she got home to quit her job. She called her supervisor at Mercy Medical Center in Springfield, Massachusetts, from wherever she was standing the moment she confirmed what she already suspected — that the Powerball ticket in her hand was worth $758.7 million. She'd worked at the hospital for 32 years. The call lasted less than a minute. That detail — not the jackpot amount, not the press conference, not the lump-sum check — is the one that stuck. It was August 2017, and in that phone call, an entire working life ended in a sentence.

That moment is the one that defines most of these stories. Not the numbers on a screen, not the official lottery announcement, but the specific, unrepeatable instant when an ordinary person realizes the world they woke up in no longer exists. The biggest lottery winners by state didn't emerge from some pattern or system. They were nurses, retirees, and young men grabbing a ticket at a gas station. And for each of them, there was a morning like Mavis's.

The Map of Luck: Which States Have Produced the Most Powerball Jackpot Winners

California and Florida Lead the Count

When you map out the largest Powerball jackpots in the game's history, two states rise above the rest: California and Florida. That's partly a function of population — more tickets sold means more chances for a winning combination to surface — but the numbers are striking nonetheless. California holds the single most remarkable entry in Powerball history: the November 8, 2022 drawing that produced a $2.04 billion jackpot, the largest lottery prize ever awarded in the United States. Florida has generated multiple jackpot winners across different draw years, earning a reputation as one of the most consistently lucky states in Powerball's footprint. Other states — Wisconsin, Massachusetts, West Virginia, Tennessee, and Illinois among them — have each produced at least one landmark winner whose story entered the national conversation.

The geography of big wins doesn't cluster in wealthy zip codes or major cities. Winning tickets have been sold in rural convenience stores, suburban supermarkets, and small-town gas stations. The map of luck, if you could call it that, looks less like a wealth map and more like a population density map — with significant, unexplained exceptions.

Before the Win: Who These People Were

Regular Lives, Regular Weeks

The week before Manuel Franco matched all six numbers in the March 2019 drawing, he was 24 years old, living in the Milwaukee area, and working a job that didn't make headlines. He was, by every public account available, a young man navigating early adulthood. Gloria MacKenzie was 84 years old when she won in Florida in 2013 — the oldest solo jackpot winner in Powerball history. She had reportedly let another shopper go ahead of her in line at a Publix supermarket before buying her ticket. That small, accidental act of courtesy is one of the more quietly astonishing footnotes in lottery history.

Jack Whittaker was already a successful businessman in West Virginia before his Christmas Day 2002 win — the owner of a pipeline and excavation company. He wasn't a struggling worker playing with spare change. But the win was still transformative, and ultimately, complicated in ways no one anticipated. And Mavis Wanczyk, who described herself as someone who had been dreaming about this moment for years, was still clocking in to care for patients right up until the moment she didn't have to anymore.

The Claim and the Chaos: 24–72 Hours After the Draw

The Window Between Knowing and the World Knowing

Most winners don't walk into lottery headquarters the next morning. There's a window — sometimes days, sometimes weeks — between the moment a winner confirms their ticket and the moment they file a claim. Attorneys get called. Financial advisors are consulted. Some winners, like Merle and Patricia Butler of Illinois, waited months before coming forward with their share of a 2012 Mega Millions jackpot. They were methodical about it in a way that impressed even lottery officials. Others move faster. Edwin Castro, the $2.04 billion California winner, claimed his prize and elected the lump-sum cash option of approximately $997.6 million before taxes — a figure that remains the largest single lottery payout in U.S. history. To understand what he actually took home after federal and state taxes, the math gets complicated quickly. Tools like a lottery tax calculator can illustrate how dramatically withholding reshapes even a ten-figure prize.

For most winners, those first 72 hours are a blur of phone calls, disbelief, and a sudden, acute awareness that their name — once public — belongs to the world. Many choose anonymity where state law allows. California, notably, did not require Castro to reveal his identity immediately, and the details of his public profile emerged gradually through official lottery channels and subsequent legal proceedings unrelated to the win itself.

The Most Human Statement From a Real Winner

"I just want to spend time with my family. Those are the only plans I have right now." — Mavis Wanczyk, at her August 2017 press conference, after being asked what she planned to do with $758.7 million.

It was not a dramatic answer. There was no mention of yachts or private islands. She said it the way someone who has worked a hospital shift every week for three decades might say it — with the particular exhaustion of someone who has been somewhere else for a very long time and is only now, finally, allowed to go home.

The Longer Arc: What the Money Did — and Didn't Do

Years Later

Jack Whittaker's story is the one that gets told most often as a cautionary tale, and it's worth treating carefully. He made documented public donations — including significant gifts to churches and charities — and expressed genuine generosity after his win. He also experienced profound personal losses in the years that followed, losses that were publicly documented and that he himself connected to the disruptions the money brought into his life. His story doesn't reduce to a simple moral, but it does complicate the idea that a large enough number solves everything it touches.

Gloria MacKenzie claimed her prize, chose the lump sum, and largely stepped away from public life — which, at 84, seemed like a reasonable decision. Manuel Franco gave a press conference in which he described feeling like he was floating, then went quiet. The public record on most winners thins out quickly after the initial announcement, which is probably how most of them prefer it.

State by State: Where the Big Wins Have Landed

For readers interested in the lottery landscape of specific states, the concentration of major winners in California — culminating in the $2.04 billion record — reflects both the state's massive ticket-buying population and its unique lottery structure. Florida has been home to multiple major jackpot winners, including Gloria MacKenzie, and continues to be one of the most active Powerball states in the country. States like Michigan have their own significant jackpot histories worth exploring — Michigan lottery records include multiple large prizes across both Powerball and Mega Millions draws over the years. Patterns Without Prophecy: What the History Reveals

What the Record Shows — and Doesn't

Looking across the documented history of the biggest lottery winners by state, a few things are genuinely observable. Large jackpots tend to cluster in high-population states, but not exclusively. Solo winners are rarer than split prizes. Most major jackpot winners in public record chose the lump sum over the annuity option, accepting a significantly smaller immediate payout in exchange for access to the full amount at once. And the gap between the advertised jackpot and what a winner actually deposits in a bank account — after the lump-sum reduction and federal and state tax withholding — is almost always larger than people expect.

None of this tells you anything useful about tomorrow's drawing. The numbers that fell on November 8, 2022, had no relationship to the numbers that fell the week before. Each drawing is its own isolated event. What the history of jackpot winners does illuminate, clearly and without embellishment, is that these moments happen to real people living ordinary lives — and that what comes after is rarely as simple as the check.
